context: acoustic & stage-commissioning-led · box-in-box structure and the fly tower drive the fit-out

brief.intro: New to this project type? A cinema, theatre or performing-arts venue is built around two things an ordinary building doesn't have: an auditorium engineered for sound, and — for live theatre — a fly tower above the stage where scenery and rigging are hoisted out of the audience's sight. The acoustic performance depends on how the structure itself is built: a "box-in-box" auditorium, isolated from the rest of the building on a floating floor and resilient wall mounts, so sound and vibration don't leak in or out. Get that structural/acoustic envelope wrong and no amount of later finishing can fix it. Once the shell and acoustic envelope are right, the programme shifts to stage machinery (rigging, hoists, revolves, an orchestra-pit lift for a theatre) or projection/screen systems for a cinema, then to AV and lighting. The true finish line is proving all of it together — an acoustic tuning pass and a live rehearsal or test screening — alongside a life-safety evacuation test sized for a packed, low-lit auditorium.

glossary.plain: the tall space above a theatre stage where scenery and lighting bars are hoisted up, out of the audience's view.
building the auditorium as its own isolated structure inside the building, so sound and vibration don't transfer in or out.
sloped seating tiers giving every seat a clear sightline to the stage or screen.
how long sound persists in a room before dying away, tuned by acoustic finishes for speech or music.
a fire-rated curtain that seals the stage opening from the auditorium in the event of a fire.
counterweight or motorised hoists carrying scenery and lighting bars over the stage.
a hydraulic platform that raises and lowers to become an orchestra pit, extra seating or a stage extension.

must_get_right: Acoustic isolation (box-in-box, floating floor, resilient mounts) is structural, not a finish — get it right before the shell closes in; it cannot be retrofitted cheaply.
Stage machinery/rigging (or projection/screen systems for a cinema) needs its own procurement and installation window before AV and acoustic commissioning can begin.
Life-safety evacuation for a packed, low-lit auditorium — fire/tab curtain, emergency lighting, voice alarm — must be proven, not just installed.
Protect real time for acoustic tuning and a live rehearsal or test event before handover; it is the actual finish line, not the last snag.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The acoustic envelope and stage-machinery packages are modelled as their own sub-networks given their sequencing and re-test risk.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and the acoustic shell run a 6-day week; MEP fit-out and stage-machinery installation move to extended hours ahead of the acoustic tuning window; commissioning runs against the availability of the acoustic consultant and a fixed rehearsal or test-event date.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs structure & fly tower → box-in-box acoustic isolation → MEP rough-in → stage machinery/rigging (or projection systems) install → AV and acoustic tuning → life-safety proving → live rehearsal / test event → handover. The acoustic envelope, not the visible finishes, gates everything that follows it.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design freeze on the acoustic envelope and stage/fly-tower rigging layout before the shell closes in; authority approvals obtained per phase gate; a single mobilisation; the acoustic consultant and stage-machinery specialist are engaged through commissioning, not just design.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is acoustic-envelope- and stage-machinery-led. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Fly-tower and rigging installation need dedicated crane/hoist access and exclusion zones below; acoustic tuning requires the building substantially quiet and finished around it, competing with the last trades on site. Skilled acoustic and stage-machinery commissioning specialists are scarce and shared across the final weeks.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: acoustic isolation defects found late (very costly to fix once the shell is closed), stage-machinery/rigging re-test loops, and acoustic-tuning re-work if background noise targets are missed. Schedule contingency is held immediately before acoustic tuning and before the life-safety proving test rather than spread thinly across finishing activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the acoustic envelope, stage machinery and commissioning — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
